    Rule-Based Strategy Engine — Audit, Architecture and Implementation Plan

    Status: working design for the chosen build. It captures the current rule-based (non-trainable) engine, the target two-layer architecture, the impact analysis across every close path and every run mode (backtest, live sim, live real), the code-quality contract, and the per-method test plan. It is a standalone reference; it assumes no prior context.

    1. Purpose and Scope

    This is a research and build line, parallel to and separate from the thesis validation work (docs/plans/EXPERIMENT_PLAN_THESIS_VALIDATION.md) and the Script 2 ensemble work (docs/plans/SCRIPT2_CLOSURE_AND_NEW_ENSEMBLE_PLAN.md). Those lines test whether trainable models find signal. This line asks a different question with a different method:

    Can a catalog of deterministic, economically-motivated trading rules — optimized by Optuna and executed through the existing engine (costs, risk, metrics, walk-forward, traceability) — produce positive net edge, with no model training?

    The end goal is a vetted battalion of strategies that run first on folds and later on multi-year data. The catalog of which strategies to implement is a parallel research effort; this document builds the engine that can host the most complex strategies possible.

    2. How the Rule-Based Model Works (current state)

    2.1 Execution model and cost

    The rule_based model (modules/model-trainer/src/rainbow/model_trainer/models/rule_based.py) is declared non-trainable in the factory (is_trainable=False, has_pre_resolved=False). A run uses one trial, no epochs, no optimizer, no backward pass, and executes evaluation and backtest through the same infrastructure as the trainable models.

    Resource profile: no GPU; CPU/RAM/disk for feature computation, parquet IO, window building, and the per-tick backtest loop. The dominant cost for a large battalion is recomputing the same features many times; sharing feature packs across strategies on the same period and bounding parallel backtests keeps it tractable. Non-trainable does not mean zero cost, and it does not mean no overfitting (Section 6).

    2.2 Expression DSL

    Rules are expression strings parsed with Python ast in a restricted, safe mode. Function calls, subscripts, lambdas, and comprehensions are rejected. Supported elements:

    • Feature references with curly-brace timestep notation: feature_name{T} (for example rsi_14{-1} is the last tick in the window). Negative indices count from the window end and are validated against the sequence length.
    • Arithmetic operators + - * / **.
    • Comparison operators < <= > >= == !=, including chained comparisons such as 30 < rsi_14{-1} < 70.
    • Boolean composition with and / or and the bitwise & / | applied to boolean results.

    Rules are evaluated in priority order; the first matching rule wins. When no rule matches, default_signal is emitted (typically NONE). Evaluation is vectorized across the batch.

    2.3 Output contract and feature coupling

    The model emits the standard contract {logits, strength, quality} with three signal classes (NONE=0, LONG=1, SHORT=2). Because the contract matches the trainable models, the same scoring, bot logic, risk manager, backtest, and metrics apply unchanged. strength and quality are currently constant for the whole rule set.

    The model does not compute indicators. A rule referencing rsi_14 only works if a feature resolving to that name already exists in the experiment's feature window. A generator preflight rejects any experiment whose rule references a missing or ambiguous feature, so coverage is validated before a run starts. Rule-feature inputs must be raw (non-normalized) so thresholds such as > 70 remain semantically valid.

    Entry rules live in config/experiments/models/rule-based-model-hyperparameters.yaml (rule_based_model_hyperparameters.rules, a list of {expression, signal}), resolved into ResolvedRuleBasedModelHyperparameters (modules/model-trainer/.../types.py).

    3. Feature Generation for Rules

    Feature blocks are built by the MEGA generator (scripts/experiments/generate/generate_mega_experiment.py). The Script 2 orchestrator delegates feature construction to MEGA via subprocess.

    3.1 Current rule_raw block: palette and limits

    The _append_rule_raw_features function emits raw features named rule_raw_{symbol}_{timeframe}_{indicator} with an empty pipeline (no normalization). Current capabilities: RSI, EMA (fast/slow), MACD (line/signal), ADX (with plus_di/minus_di), Stochastic (k_percent) — five families toggled by include_* flags; exactly one timeframe per experiment; per-symbol builder (BTC 5m shipped). Raw OHLCV is ensured as input but not exposed as a named rule feature. Net effect: prior rule-based experiments were single-timeframe, single-symbol, five-indicator only.

    3.2 Full indicator catalog (available, not yet wired to rules)

    The indicator library (modules/data-processing/src/rainbow/data_processing/indicator/) already implements more than the five wired families:

    Indicator Selectable columns Scaling
    ADX adx, plus_di, minus_di ADX 0–100; DI unbounded
    ATR atr Raw, price units
    Bollinger Bands upper_band, middle_band, lower_band, percent_b, bandwidth Bands raw; percent_b 0–1
    Correlation correlation -1..1
    Drawdown drawdown, max_drawdown -1..0
    EMA ema Raw, price units
    MACD macd, signal, histogram Raw, unbounded
    OBV obv Raw, cumulative
    Price Oscillator oscillator Raw, unbounded
    Ratio ratio Raw, unbounded
    RSI rsi 0–100
    Spread spread Raw (optionally normalized)
    Stochastic k_percent, d_percent 0–100
    Time Features 10 sin/cos channels -1..1
    Volatility volatility Raw, non-negative
    VWAP vwap Raw, price units

    Bounded indicators take fixed thresholds directly (rsi_14{-1} > 70). Raw/price indicators are best used in comparisons (close{-1} > vwap{-1}, ema_9{-1} > ema_21{-1}).

    4. Backtest and Live Execution Model

    The backtest trades a single instrument: the experiment's base_symbol. Extra symbols are consumed only as context features; no positions are opened on them. Contextual multi-symbol (use ETH/BNB features to decide a BTC trade) is supported; portfolio multi-symbol is not. Execution realism is present: maker/taker commission split, slippage with variability, minimum-notional rejection, full investor metrics including benchmark and risk-constrained alpha.

    Live trading reuses the same bot decision code: runtime_loop calls the same generate_entry_signals / generate_exit_orders as the backtest, and the same apply_trailing_stops. LIVE_SIM fills orders through a simulated adapter; LIVE_REAL routes to a provider adapter whose submit_order is not yet implemented (providers return rejected), with no slippage, no partial close, and no persisted pending queue (Section 8.2).

    5. Bot Decision Flow

    Entries (modules/bot-logic/src/rainbow/bot_logic/bot_logic.py, generate_entry_signals) turn the signal plus strength/quality into proposals gated by entry_threshold, min_quality_threshold, same_direction_cooldown_ticks, signal_flip_threshold, and require_higher_confidence, then sized by the risk manager. strength scales take-profit distance, quality tightens the stop, and both influence size. These gates are fixed (not an expressible rule engine).

    Exits (generate_exit_orders) are priority-ordered and config-driven, first-match-wins per position: stop loss → take profit → signal flip → uncertainty (side confidence below exit_threshold), plus risk force-flat (applied in the engine loop) and optional end-of-window liquidation. Stop loss and take profit are gated by exit_enabled. A build_close_order factory (helpers/exit_manager.py) composes the typed CLOSE order, and orders.py processes any CLOSE order generically (slippage, PnL, persistence) — so new exit reasons reuse the entire close path without engine changes.

    The three-class signal has no CLOSE: NONE means "do not open", it does not close a position. "Enter on A, exit on B" cannot be expressed as A -> LONG, B -> NONE; the exit must map to a bot mechanism. The bot also does not receive raw features at decision time — only the prediction, positions, price, and time.

    6. Remaining Limitations

    The trailing stop, previously inert, now applies and persists per tick in both backtest (engine_loop.py, apply_trailing_stops) and live (runtime_loop), with a TRAILING_STOP exit code. Remaining limitations that this plan addresses:

    6.1 DSL / model limits

    • No function calls (abs, min, max); no rolling statistics inside an expression.
    • No position awareness inside a rule (entry price, bars-since-entry, unrealized PnL are available to the bot but not exposed to rule expressions).
    • No explicit CLOSE action; only NONE/LONG/SHORT.
    • strength/quality are constant for a whole rule set, limiting confidence-based sizing and pyramiding.
    • Rules use priority (first match wins), not voting.
    • The numbers inside rule strings are plain literals, not Optuna-optimized; parameter search is grids only.

    6.2 Flaws in the shipped rule configuration

    The previously-shipped configuration stacked classic rules in priority order. Two design problems make its negative results uninformative about rule viability: shadowing (with first-match-wins, the EMA fast-vs-slow pair captures almost every row, so MACD/ADX/Stochastic rules never fire) and state, not event (ema_9{-1} > ema_21{-1} detects a persistent state, not a crossover; a crossover needs two timesteps). These produce persistent directional signals, not discrete entry events.

    7. Target Architecture — Two Layers

    A professional trader answers two distinct questions every tick. The engine mirrors that with two layers, each isolated, with one clear responsibility and a well-defined interface.

    7.1 Layer 1 — Market view (the model) — unchanged

    Layer 1 answers "what does the market look like now?" and produces the signal LONG/SHORT/NONE plus strength/quality, from market features only. It is not position-aware. It is the model — rule_based (view by rules) or a trainable (view by network). Its output is cached in the prediction parquet and flows into the thesis pipeline and ensembles. This layer is not changed by this work; the training contract is untouched.

    7.2 Layer 2 — Action engine (the bot) — universal, position-aware

    Layer 2 answers "given that view and my current book, what do I do?" and produces actions. It is position-aware (open positions, unrealized PnL, bars-since-entry, free slots, exposure) and runs in the bot at runtime. It is a universal bot feature: it consumes the Layer-1 signal of any model — rule_based, mlp, tcn, vit — because the bot is shared by all models and does not depend on which model produced the signal. No model is modified to gain it.

    Today Layer 2 is a set of fixed gates plus the fixed exit priority (Section 5). The target is to make Layer 2 an expressible rule-driven action engine over the shared DSL, while the existing fixed gates remain the default behavior when no rules are configured.

    7.3 The shared rule DSL — rainbow.common.rules

    The expression evaluator currently lives inside rule_based.py (model-trainer). It is extracted into a new shared subpackage modules/common/src/rainbow/common/rules/ so both layers reuse one evaluator without violating dependency direction (bot-logic must not import model-trainer):

    • A rule type (expression: str, an action literal, optional per-rule strength/quality).
    • A safe AST compiler (the current allow-list) that compiles an expression once.
    • An evaluator that runs a compiled expression against a supplied variable context — either a batch of feature tensors (Layer 1, the model) or a single-tick scalar context of features plus position variables (Layer 2, the bot).
    • A placeholder binding step (${param}) for Optuna (Section 7.5).

    Model-trainer's rule_based imports the evaluator from common.rules for Layer 1; bot-logic imports it for Layer 2. One evaluator, in the foundation layer, shared.

    The DSL is expressive — operators live in the DSL, heavy transforms live in features. The split rule: cheap, ad-hoc, short-window logic is a DSL operator; heavy, reused, or long-history logic is a precomputed feature that a rule just references.

    • DSL operators: single offsets feature{-1}; range selectors feature{-20:-2} and disjoint lists feature{-60:-50,-20:-1}; window aggregates over a range (highest, lowest, avg, sum, min, max, std, count, any, all); scalar functions (abs, min, max); event/series helpers (bars_since, cross_up, cross_down, change, pct_change, consecutive_true, slope, percentile); plus arithmetic, comparisons, and booleans.
    • Feature/signal layer (already rich — data-processing/signals/ provides crossover, z-score, threshold, and an expression-based condition signal): heavy or reused transforms — long-window z-scores, correlations, spreads, volatility-normalized series, regime labels, complex reused boolean conditions. A rule references these as ordinary features; it does not recompute them.

    This operator set is a superset of the current rule_based grammar (which rejects function calls and has no ranges), so the rule_based migration (Phase 1, run after the live ensemble) gains ranges and functions rather than staying at parity. Conditions such as NR7 or inside-bar then need no new feature — they fall out of the DSL (true_range{-1} == lowest(true_range{-7:-1}), high{-1} < high{-2} and low{-1} > low{-2}).

    7.4 Action set (Layer 2)

    The action engine evaluates rules (with market + position context) and emits, per position and per free slot, one of:

    Action Meaning
    ENTER_LONG / ENTER_SHORT open a new position (position-aware: respects book state)
    ADD pyramid into a position moving in favor
    REDUCE scale out a portion (e.g. partial take-profit)
    CLOSE close a position (reuses build_close_order; exit code RULE_EXIT)
    REVERSE close and open the opposite side
    MOVE_STOP / MODIFY_TP edit a position's protective levels (break-even, ratchet)
    ENABLE_TRAIL / UPDATE_TRAIL turn on or adjust the trailing stop
    FLAT_AT_TIME force-flat at a session boundary
    HOLD do nothing

    CLOSE is the first action implemented (the parallel close channel); the others extend the same engine (Section 11). Entry actions in Layer 2 are position-aware and complement — do not replace — the Layer-1 market view: Layer 1 says the market is LONG, Layer 2 decides whether and how to act given the book.

    A regime-switch strategy is expressible natively — conditions over the regime feature with and/or (e.g. regime_trend_trending{-1}==1 and cross_up(...) for the trend sub-policy, regime_range... for the mean-reversion one), no new engine capability; rule grouping would be optional sugar only. Note the order-layer cost (Section 8.1): CLOSE reuses the existing generic close path, but ADD, REDUCE, REVERSE, MOVE_STOP, and MODIFY_TP require new order actions and are scheduled in Phase 4.

    7.5 Parametric rules + Optuna over strategy parameters

    A rule may carry tunable placeholders, e.g. rsi_14{-1} < ${rsi_buy}. A strategy declares a search space over its placeholders reusing the existing Optuna param kinds (Float/Int/Ranges/Categorical/log). Each trial binds the placeholders, builds the concrete rules, runs the backtest, and is scored by alpha_rc/net.

    There are two optimizers, one per layer, because the layers live in different places and have different cost profiles. The native Optuna inside model-trainer today samples only the model and its training (learning rate, batch size, weight decay, loss, architecture, feature selection); it does not touch the bot, and for the non-trainable rule_based it optimizes nothing (the rule thresholds are fixed literals, so it runs a single deterministic trial). The bot-config optimizer (scripts/thesis/script_2_thesis/bot_config_optimizer) is a separate script that varies the bot_config over cached predictions. Strategy optimization maps onto these two homes:

    Layer What is optimized Optimizer Cost Status today
    Layer 1 (view / signal) entry-rule thresholds (change the signal) extension of the native model-trainer Optuna — make it sample the rule placeholders for rule_based and regenerate the signal per trial (no training) regenerates the signal each trial; no training not built — the native Optuna does not sample rule params yet
    Layer 2 (actions / bot) action-rule params + stops/TP/sizing (do not change the signal) the bot-config optimizer (script) over cached predictions re-backtest only, fast exists

    So optimizing the market view is an extension of the native model Optuna (it belongs to the signal flow); optimizing execution and management is the existing separate optimizer. Each layer keeps its natural home and reuses the shared param kinds and suggest_* machinery; neither is forced into the other.

    Overfitting control is mandatory and identical to a grid: tune in-fold, validate out-of-fold / on a held-out window, before any parameter set is believed. (The first profitable Jun-19 result is in-sample and unproven until validated out-of-fold.)

    7.6 A strategy as one object

    A strategy is defined in one place as {entry_rules (Layer 1), action_rules (Layer 2), param_space}, all in the same DSL. At experiment generation it is deployed to its technical homes: entry rules to the model hyperparameters, action rules to bot_config. The single definition gives coherence; the split homes respect the cacheable-signal vs runtime-position-aware nature of each layer.

    8. Impact Analysis

    8.1 Backtest decision and close paths

    Per tick, process_tick (engine_loop.py) runs: execute pending orders → resolve prediction → apply_trailing_stops → generate_exit_orders → risk force-flat → generate_entry_signals → queue orders; end-of-run liquidation runs after the loop. Existing exit codes (common/types/trade_meta.py): STOP_LOSS, TAKE_PROFIT, TRAILING_STOP, SIGNAL_FLIP, LOW_CONFIDENCE, MANUAL. The action engine plugs into generate_exit_orders (for CLOSE/REDUCE/REVERSE) and generate_entry_signals (for ENTER/ADD), reusing build_close_order and the generic CLOSE path in orders.py. A new RULE_EXIT exit code is added. CLOSE needs no orders.py change (the generic close path handles it); ADD, REDUCE, REVERSE, MOVE_STOP, and MODIFY_TP need new order actions in orders.py (today only OPEN/CLOSE) and in the live execution adapters — real work scheduled in Phase 4, beyond just passing features (Section 8.3).

    8.2 Live (sim + real)

    Live reuses the same generate_exit_orders / generate_entry_signals, so the action engine is inherited by both live modes once the bot decision code carries it. LIVE_SIM fills via the simulated adapter (queued with latency, seeded slippage) — works. LIVE_REAL has known gaps, recorded so they are not a surprise: submit_order is not implemented (providers return rejected), no slippage is applied, partial close is rejected, and the pending queue is not persisted across restart. The action engine therefore runs correctly in backtest and LIVE_SIM; in LIVE_REAL it inherits these gaps. This is not a blocker because strategies are validated on folds first; LIVE_REAL execution and reconciliation are a separate prerequisite for going live.

    8.3 Model→bot contract and feature passing

    Layer 1's contract ({logits, strength, quality} and derived prob_*/combined_confidence) is unchanged — no close_signal is added to the model, so the prediction parquet, ensemble merge, and frontend types are untouched. Layer 2 needs the raw features of the tick and the position variables. The bot does not receive features today, so generate_exit_orders and generate_entry_signals gain a typed feature-context parameter, supplied by the engine loop (backtest) and the runtime loop (live) — both already hold the feature row. Position variables (bars_since_entry, unrealized_pnl_pct, entry_price) are derived from the open position the bot already has.

    8.4 Resume / pause state

    CLOSE/exit rules are stateless and need no new persisted state. Stateful actions (e.g. a per-position pyramid counter, or a "scaled out once" flag) must be persisted in the runtime state (resume_state.py backtest, runtime_state_json live) to survive pause/resume; the design keeps Layer-2 rule state explicit and serialized when an action requires it.

    8.5 Files touched vs not touched

    Touched Why

    common/types/trade_meta.py add RULE_EXIT exit code
    common/types/configs/experiments/bot_config.py + config/experiments/bot.yaml Layer-2 action-rules config (follows the StopLossConfig.exit_enabled pattern)
    bot-logic/helpers/ (new evaluator-driven action helper) + bot_logic.py evaluate action rules; plug into entry/exit generation; new feature-context param

    9. Code Quality Contract

    Every change in this line meets the project standard; messy-but-working is not acceptable.

    • Typed objects, not dicts. Rules, contexts, and results are Pydantic models / frozen dataclasses passed whole; flatten to columns only at the persistence boundary. Variable names follow the type (action_rule, not rule).
    • Placement by responsibility. Shared DSL in rainbow.common.rules (foundation layer); action helpers with the other bot-logic helpers; the exit code with the other exit codes; config sub-models with the other bot config. Dependency direction respected: bot-logic imports common, never model_trainer.
    • Reuse, do not duplicate. Reuse build_close_order/build_exit_meta_from_bot/build_exit_reason, the CLOSE path in orders.py, the Optuna suggest_value/suggest_override, the existing config-loading and param kinds. Extract the DSL once and share it; never copy the evaluator.
    • No suppression, no legacy, no patches. Fix root causes; no type: ignore/noqa/pylint: disable; no _old/compatibility shims; remove what a change replaces.
    • Docs and comments as code. Full docstrings (params, returns, examples); comments explain the non-obvious why. No meta-language (no narrating changes, no before/after, no plan/phase references in code, docstrings, or commit messages).
    • Quality gates per file (src and tests): ruff check, mypy --strict, pyright clean, pylint ≥ 9.5, markdownlint for docs. Mirrored by the per-module linting-gate test.

    10. Test Plan

    Every new method has tests; every change is covered. Each unit is tested for positive, edge, and negative cases, following the existing per-module test layout and the linting-gate test that runs the quality gates over src and tests.

    • DSL (common.rules): parse/compile valid expressions (positive); chained comparisons, negative timesteps, placeholder binding (edge); rejected AST nodes, unknown/ambiguous feature, out-of-range timestep, malformed placeholder (negative). Evaluate against both a batch context and a single-tick position-aware context.
    • Action engine (bot-logic): each action fires when its rule matches (positive); first-match/priority interaction with the fixed exits, exact-threshold boundaries, position-variable values at entry/edge (edge); no duplicate close of the same position, no entry while force-closing, action with no matching rule → HOLD (negative). Reuse of build_close_order verified (exit code RULE_EXIT, metadata correct).
    • Config: model loads from YAML with defaults; rejects out-of-range; absent block → fixed-gate default behavior unchanged.
    • Feature passing: the engine loop and runtime loop deliver the correct feature context to the bot; parity between backtest and live for the same inputs.
    • Optuna: search space samples valid configs; placeholder binding produces the intended rules; a Layer-2 trial reuses cached predictions while a Layer-1 trial regenerates the signal; objective reads the produced session metrics.
    • Resume: a stateful action's state round-trips through pause/resume unchanged.
    • Trailing-stop invariant: a regression test that locks the current trailing behavior (the stop moves and persists; TRAILING_STOP exit fires) so the rule-based work cannot silently regress it.

    11. Incremental Implementation Roadmap

    Build the abstraction once; deliver in slices so each slice is shippable and validated.

    1. Phase 1 — Shared DSL. Extract the evaluator into rainbow.common.rules (rule type + AST compiler + context evaluator + placeholder binding). Migrate rule_based to import it (no behavior change) — the migration runs after the live ensemble to avoid disturbing it. Tests + gates.
    2. Phase 2 — Parallel close channel. Layer-2 CLOSE action: config sub-model, action helper, plug into generate_exit_orders, RULE_EXIT code, feature-context passing through engine/runtime loops, position-aware variables. Tests across backtest + live sim. This is the first instance of the action engine.
    3. Phase 3 — Optuna over strategy params. Parametric placeholders + search space; Layer-2 optimization over cached predictions (reuse bot-config optimizer); Layer-1 signal-regeneration loop; in-fold/out-of-fold validation harness.
    4. Phase 4 — Position-aware entries and management. ENTER/ADD/REDUCE/REVERSE actions as extensions of the same engine; stateful-action persistence.
    5. Phase 5 — Feature layer + catalog. Expose far more of the existing feature/signal system to rule experiments (today rule_raw is the bottleneck: 5 raw indicators, single timeframe) across timeframes, periods, context symbols, and raw OHLCV. Add the classic indicators still missing from the 16-indicator catalog — Williams %R, CCI, MFI, PPO, TRIX, Keltner, SuperTrend, Aroon, Ichimoku, Parabolic SAR, Choppiness, plus swing/structure features (fractals, pivots) — each a self-contained data-processing/.../indicator/<name>.py on the existing process_<name> mold (the polars-ta library covers most), wired into IndicatorType, the dispatch, the MEGA generator, and tests. This wave also adds a REGIME / MARKET_STATE indicator: the detector's compute_indicators + classify_regime logic is moved into data-processing as a composite indicator emitting the three regime axes as binary features (trend / volatility / direction → the 27/9/3 taxonomies by combination). It is used at whatever timeframe is set in the experiment config (e.g. 1d), exactly like any other indicator — the existing multi-timeframe handling makes a higher-timeframe feature usable at the base timeframe, so there is no new alignment work. The offline regime scripts under scripts/analysis/regime/ then import that one shared implementation instead of keeping their own copy — a single source of truth for the regime definition. Then a Phase-0 control battery and the vetted battalion on folds → chronological holdout → multi-year (the multi-year step needs the data refresh + de-hardcoded folds noted in the master roadmap).

    12. Decisions and Open Questions

    Decisions taken:

    • CLOSE and all Layer-2 actions live in the bot, not in the model; the Layer-1 training contract is not touched.
    • The DSL is extracted to a new rainbow.common.rules subpackage and shared by both layers.
    • Layer 2 is a universal bot feature available to any model, not specific to rule_based.
    • Position-awareness is in scope from the start.
    • Optuna optimizes both layers; overfitting is controlled by in-fold tune / out-of-fold validation.
    • The DSL is expressive (range selectors + window aggregates + scalar and event functions); heavy or reused transforms stay in the feature/signal layer.
    • Track A adds the classic indicators missing from the catalog (Williams %R, CCI, MFI, PPO, TRIX, Keltner, SuperTrend, Aroon, Ichimoku, Parabolic SAR, Choppiness, fractals, pivots) on the existing indicator mold.
    • Regime is exposed as a REGIME / MARKET_STATE indicator: the detector's classify_regime is moved into data-processing (the three axes as binary features, used at a configurable timeframe like any indicator), and the offline regime scripts reuse that one implementation. Regime-switch is expressed with conditions over these features, not a grouping capability.

    Open questions:

    • Action priority/conflict resolution between the rule engine and the existing fixed exits (which wins when both fire).
    • Exact set of position variables and feature context exposed to Layer-2 rules in the first slice.
    • Whether Layer-1 and Layer-2 parameters are optimized jointly or in stages.
    • Per-symbol battalions vs contextual multi-symbol; lab folder name for the catalog.

    14. Parallel research: the strategy catalog

    Which strategies to implement is a separate research effort that defines the rules and actions to express; it does not change the engine architecture above. A 50-strategy seed catalog exists (docs/_researchs/_RULE_BASED/), grouped by family and weighted by evidence: trend-following / breakout / time-series momentum are the strongest, trend-filtered pullback and intermarket confirmation next, and mean-reversion is useful but cost-fragile. Each strategy references one of eight reusable bot profiles (trend-rider, breakout, pullback, mean-reversion, intraday/VWAP, failure-reversal, spread/pairs, regime-switch hybrid) that template the management logic.

    Coverage with this plan (expressive DSL + the added indicators + the Layer-2 action engine): essentially the whole single-instrument catalog is expressible. NR7 and inside-bar need no new feature (they fall out of the DSL); the missing classic indicators are Phase-5 additions on the existing mold. The only strategy deferred by structure is two-leg pairs / spread execution — it needs synchronized long-short legs and shared-capital accounting (a portfolio-execution capability), not an indicator or a DSL feature. Regime-switch hybrids are expressible natively (conditions over a REGIME feature; no grouping needed), and session/VWAP strategies need session features plus FLAT_AT_TIME; both are achievable, not deferred by structure.

    Each strategy becomes one experiment, recorded in an experiment ledger with: strategy family, base-logic id, parameter variant, feature profile, symbol-context profile, execution profile, and source hypothesis — so robustness scoring (with deflated-Sharpe / PBO multiple-testing control) sees the whole tested family, not just the winners.
